shots.narration: A puff adder bit a honey badger on the face.
Five hours later, it hunted snakes again.
Doug ends up behind a honey badger, facing six lions.
Its plan doesn't include him.
The Puff Adder.
A honey badger's muscles have a lock that cobra-type nerve toxins can't easily open.
Those toxins work by gripping a receptor that muscles use to take orders from nerves.
In the honey badger, one small part of that receptor carries a positive charge,
so the toxin struggles to hold on.
Colleen Begg, who spent years following wild honey badgers, came across the bitten badger with its cheek badly swollen.
A puff adder is a heavy African viper that waits in ambush, about as long as a baseball bat,
and honey badgers hunt them and eat them.
Here's the problem.
A puff adder is not a cobra, and its venom attacks tissue instead,
so that receptor is not what it aims at and the famous trick is no help here.
The badger just takes the swelling and waits it out,
because resistant is not the same thing as immune.
Hedgehogs and pigs evolved almost the same change in that receptor on their own,
while mongooses blocked the same spot in a different way, by coating it in sugar molecules.
Mammals have jammed that one lock at least four separate times.
Doug was handed the other end of the same snake, for science, while the badger held the end with the teeth.
Doug did not agree to this.
Doug has died. Again.

elements.text: BADGER: SWELLS UP. 5 HOURS. BACK TO WORK.

shots.narration: Only one of them had the right muscles, and neither of them had read the paper.

elements.text: BADGER: SWELLS UP. 5 HOURS. BACK TO WORK.

shots.narration: Next, the badger goes after something with no fangs at all, just a whole colony of stingers.
Smaller.
The Hive.
For more than two hundred years, people have told a story about a bird that leads honey badgers to bees' nests,
and scientists still have no solid record of it.
Honey badgers really do raid bees' nests and will climb trees to reach them,
and they want the larvae inside as much as the honey.
The bird is the greater honeyguide, a brown bird that weighs about as much as an egg.
In the story, it leads a badger to a nest and eats the wax once the badger breaks in.
Here is the strange part.
The story goes back to a traveller called Anders Sparrman in seventeen eighty-five,
and he never saw it himself, only heard it from local people.
In two thousand twenty-three, a team interviewed three hundred and ninety-four honey-hunters across nine African countries.
Most had never seen it, though many in some Tanzanian communities had,
and the team's best guess is that it is rare, very local, or both.
The bird does guide one animal for certain.
In Mozambique, Yao honey-hunters call it with a loud trill and a short grunt,
and in an experiment that call doubled their chance of being guided.
Doug followed a honeyguide, expecting a badger to meet him at the nest and do the dangerous part.
The bird did exactly what it does. It guides people.
No badger came, and the bees did.
Doug has died. Again.
The bird got its wax.
The next animal on the list doesn't want honey at all, only whatever the badger digs up.
The Jackal.
In the Kalahari, a digging honey badger often has a jackal right behind it,
waiting for something to run out of the hole.
Black-backed jackals weigh about eight kilograms, a little less than the badger, and they are not here to fight it.
A badger hunts with its nose in the ground,
so anything that bolts from the dig gets grabbed by whoever happens to be standing closest.
Colleen and Keith Begg followed nine wild badgers for years.
Seven other species tagged along to feed, and the most common were black-backed jackals and pale chanting goshawks,
a hawk that will perch near a badger's den and wait for it to come out.
A badger can cover up to twenty-seven kilometers in a day, which is further than a half marathon,
mostly with its face in a hole.
The odd part is how little the badger does about it.
With the hawks, the badger lost nothing anyone could measure.
The jackals cost it about five percent of its prey overall, all of it caught above ground,
so it mostly just keeps digging.
Doug joined the freeloaders with a small bowl and waited by the hole.
The jackal got the gerbil, and Doug got a face full of dirt.
Doug is fine.
The narrator had built this whole stop around the jackal, and the jackal was not interested in Doug at all.
The badger lets small things follow it around, but anything that tries to hold on to it meets a very different animal.
Its size.
The Skin.
Grab a honey badger by the scruff, and it can turn round inside its own skin to bite you.
The skin is thick and loose.
Near the throat it is about six millimeters thick, roughly a stack of eight bank cards,
and the only thin skin is on the belly.
It hangs on the body like an oversized hoodie,
so if you grab the hood, the person inside still has room to turn round and face you.
That is the badger's whole plan for being caught.
Begg puts it simply: even when a predator gets hold of one, the loose skin lets it twist round and bite back.
Zoologists also describe that skin as keeping out some bee stings, some snake fangs and some teeth.
An average Kalahari male weighs about nine kilograms, and males are about a third bigger than females,
which makes this a small animal that is built to be a bad thing to hold.
Here's the catch.
Most handles are meant to give you control,
but on a honey badger the scruff is just more loose skin, and the badger inside it is already turning round.
Doug read a card called How to Hold a Badger, and the card said scruff.
Doug has died. Again.
Big cats have to deal with the same skin, and some of them have found ways around it.
Bigger.
The Leopard.
Leopards kill honey badgers, and so do lions,
so the idea that nothing hunts this animal is simply wrong.
In the southern Kalahari, the Beggs recorded lions, leopards and probably spotted hyenas killing both adult badgers and cubs,
and the black-backed jackals from earlier killed cubs too.
A male leopard in Kruger National Park averages about fifty-eight kilograms.
Leopards prefer prey between ten and forty kilograms.
A nine kilogram badger weighs a little less than a full ten-litre bucket of water, just under the size they like best.
When the Beggs looked at the badgers' fights with other carnivores, the winner could mostly be predicted from body size,
and on this scale the badger has stopped being the big one.
The uncomfortable part is what the badger does about it.
Begg has watched badgers sniff fresh lion or leopard tracks and bolt for a hole,
which means the famous fearless animal checks the ground for cats and then leaves.
Doug crossed out two words in his field guide with a sigh, and looked around for the leopard.
The leopard was in the tree above him, and it was not there for the badger.
Doug has died. Again.
From here the scale only goes up, and the next attacker on it is Doug himself.
The Beekeeper.
In one survey of beekeepers in South Africa's Western Cape, about half admitted to killing honey badgers.
About four in five said badgers had caused them problems,
because badgers climb, they break hives open, and an unprotected apiary is a row of easy meals.
A beekeeper is the heaviest attacker yet, since Doug weighs eighty kilograms,
about eight full buckets of water, and the badgers were still winning.
Here is the twist.
The fix was not a weapon.
In two thousand two, the Endangered Wildlife Trust and the bee industry launched a badger-friendly programme.
Hives went up on stands a badger could not climb, or were secured so they could not be pushed over or opened.
It grew into a national accreditation,
and Woolworths, a big South African retailer, put its honey under a badger-friendly code of practice.
Raising and securing hives can cut losses significantly, and nobody has to fight anything.
Doug built a hive stand with legs that only a cartoonist could love,
and the badger walked under it, sniffed once, and left.
Doug is fine.
So far, the only thing in this video to beat a honey badger is furniture,
and lions don't get furniture.
Lions.
The Lion.
At Kapama, a private reserve in South Africa, a ranger watched a young lioness go for an adult honey badger,
get nowhere, and quickly give up.
A lioness averages about one hundred and twenty-six kilograms and a male about one hundred and ninety,
which is thirteen to twenty badgers, or a long line of full buckets.
The same morning showed why a lion might not bother.
Her brother had already caught a young badger, and then a stench reached the vehicle,
and the male lion stopped eating and walked away from his own meal.
Honey badgers have two large scent glands under the tail.
People have smelled them from more than forty-five meters away, nearly the length of an Olympic pool.
The worst part, for the lion, is the maths.
There is skin it can't get a grip on, an animal that turns round and bites,
and a smell bad enough to put a male lion off a meal it had already won.
Lions do kill honey badgers. They just have to want it.
Doug hid behind a honey badger,
and the lion sniffed them both, thought about it for a while, and left.
Doug is fine. The narrator had a lion booked for this slot.
It works on one lion, but the next stop has six of them.
The Pride.
In two thousand twelve, a ranger at Kapama watched one honey badger run straight at six lions.
Six lions, and one adult lioness alone weighs about as much as thirteen badgers, or thirteen full buckets of water.
He had gone out looking for lions and found them on the road, apparently playing with each other.
They were not playing.
A male honey badger was charging straight at them, teeth showing, groaning as it came.
The lions did not seem to know what to do.
The badger ran right through the middle of the pride,
and when it reached a young male, it growled and swung a front paw at his face.
Then it did the thing that actually saved it, which was to go down a hole in the ground,
and after a while the lions lost interest and wandered off.
Here is the real secret of the fearless honey badger.
Its first plan is to leave.
Begg describes badgers that avoid trouble wherever they can,
and usually only attack when a predator surprises them, often while they are digging with their noses in the ground.
Caught out in the open, they stand their ground, but given a hole, they take the hole.
Doug stood behind the badger in front of six lions, and the badger went down the hole.
Doug did not fit.
Doug has died. Again.
The badger was never planning to share the hole.
In the morning, the badger came out of the hole and found the cap lying on the sand.
It sniffed the cap once,
decided it was not worth the trouble, and left it there.
Doug deaths: three hundred and ninety-one.
Subscribe, and see which animal decides Doug is worth the trouble next.
